paragraphs.heading: A current driven by weight
paragraphs.text: Thermohaline circulation is part of the ocean's planet-wide flow. It is driven by differences in how dense seawater is from place to place, and those differences come from heat and fresh water gained or lost at the surface. The name joins thermo-, for temperature, and haline, for salt, the two things that together decide how heavy seawater is. It is often called the ocean conveyor belt, a phrase coined by the climate scientist Wallace Smith Broecker.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs.text: The moving water carries heat, along with dissolved solids and gases, all around the globe. So the state of this circulation has a large effect on Earth's climate. It has two main limbs: the Atlantic meridional overturning circulation, or AMOC, in the north Atlantic, and the Southern Ocean overturning circulation near Antarctica. The AMOC has been studied far more because 90% of people live in the Northern Hemisphere, yet the southern limb matters just as much for climate.

paragraphs.heading: How heat and salt set density
paragraphs.text: Wind has long been known to push ocean currents, but only near the surface. Warm water is lighter than cold water, and salty water is heavier than fresh water. Fresh water is densest at 4 °C, but seawater keeps getting denser as it cools, right down to its freezing point. That freezing point can sit below −2 °C, depending on salt and pressure. Normally the Sun warms the ocean from above, so light warm water floats on cold dense water in layers; wind and tides stir these layers, and that mixing is what lets deep currents form.

paragraphs.heading: Sinking in the North Atlantic
paragraphs.text: The North Atlantic is one of the few parts of the ocean where evaporation outweighs rain and snow, partly because it is so windy. Evaporation leaves the salt behind, so the surface water there is unusually salty. The region is already cool, and evaporation cools the water further. This heavy water sinks in the Norwegian Sea, fills the Arctic basin and spills south through gaps in the ridge joining Greenland, Iceland and Great Britain. The narrow, shallow Bering Strait keeps it from reaching the Pacific. Instead it moves slowly into the deep plains of the south Atlantic.

paragraphs.heading: Sinking around Antarctica
paragraphs.text: Near Antarctica, strong winds rushing off the continent sweep new sea ice away and open patches of bare water called polynyas. Without its ice cover, the water there is cooled hard. As fresh ice forms, pure water freezes first and leaves salty brine behind, a process called brine rejection. The resulting Antarctic bottom water sinks and moves north and east. It is denser even than the North Atlantic water, so it travels underneath it.

paragraphs.heading: Signs of slowing
paragraphs.text: Evidence suggests both limbs are slowing as climate change melts ice sheets and freshens the water. A full collapse of either one to a much weaker state would be an example of a climate tipping point. One hemisphere would then face more droughts while the other got wetter, and a collapsed AMOC would make many European countries much colder. Such a collapse is generally thought to be more than a century away, though these forecasts are very uncertain.
